Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 8 of 10): Total War and the First Cracks, 1914–1938

Summary: The First World War pulled millions of soldiers and labourers from across the empire into the fighting, and Britain came out of it with its largest-ever territory, including new mandates in the Middle East. But the same years brought the Easter Rising, the Amritsar massacre, revolution in Egypt, revolt in Iraq, Irish independence, Gandhi's mass campaigns and the Arab Revolt in Palestine. This post covers 1914 to 1938, when the empire was at its biggest and its foundations were already cracking.

---

## The big picture

The empire went to war in August 1914 as a single unit. When Britain declared war, India, the dominions and the colonies were all automatically at war too. Over the next four years the empire raised around 8.7 million troops, including roughly 1.4 million from India (about 1.3 million served overseas), over 600,000 from Canada, over 400,000 from Australia and over 100,000 from New Zealand, plus large African carrier corps and labour units from China, Egypt and the Caribbean.

The war also produced contradictory promises in the Middle East: to Arab leaders, to France, and to the Zionist movement. After the war Britain gained mandates over Palestine, Transjordan and Iraq, and took over German colonies in Africa. The empire reached its greatest extent around 1920 to 1922.

But wartime sacrifices led to demands for self-rule, and the US president Woodrow Wilson's language of "self-determination" travelled further than he intended. 1919 was a year of crisis across the empire.

## Main timeline: the First World War (1914–1918)

| Date | What happened | Where |
|---|---|---|
| August 1914 | Britain declares war (4 August); the empire is at war automatically | Global |
| September 1914 | **Komagata Maru** returns from Canada with Punjabi migrants who were refused entry; police kill around 20 at Budge Budge | Canada and Bengal |
| October 1914 | Indian troops in the trenches in Flanders; Maritz Rebellion of Boer veterans in South Africa | Europe and South Africa |
| November 1914 | Ottomans enter the war; British-Indian troops land at Basra | Mesopotamia |
| December 1914 | Egypt declared a British protectorate | Egypt |
| January 1915 | **John Chilembwe's rising** | Nyasaland |
| February 1915 | **Singapore Mutiny** of Indian troops; the Ghadar Party's planned uprising in Punjab is betrayed | Singapore and India |
| April 1915 to January 1916 | **Gallipoli**; ANZAC landings (25 April) | Ottoman Empire |
| 1915–1916 | Hussein–McMahon correspondence promises Arab independence | Middle East |
| April 1916 | **Easter Rising** in Dublin; the surrender at **Kut** in Mesopotamia | Ireland and Iraq |
| May 1916 | Sykes–Picot Agreement divides the Middle East between Britain and France | Middle East |
| June 1916 | Arab Revolt begins under Sharif Hussein | Arabia |
| July 1916 | The Somme begins | France |
| 1916–1917 | Uprisings across the Niger Delta and northern Nigeria (e.g. Iseyin 1916) against wartime pressure | Nigeria |
| March 1917 | Baghdad taken | Iraq |
| August 1917 | Montagu Declaration promises "responsible government" for India gradually | India |
| October 1917 | Australian Light Horse charge at Beersheba | Palestine |
| November 1917 | **Balfour Declaration** (2 November) | Palestine |
| December 1917 | Allenby enters Jerusalem | Palestine |
| 1918 | Influenza pandemic; India loses perhaps 12 to 20 million people | Global |
| November 1918 | Armistice (11 November) | Europe |
| December 1918 | Sinn Féin wins most Irish seats in the general election | Ireland |

## Main timeline: the crisis years (1919–1922)

| Date | What happened | Where |
|---|---|---|
| January 1919 | First Dáil meets; the Irish War of Independence begins (21 January) | Ireland |
| March 1919 | Rowlatt Act extends wartime detention powers; **Egyptian Revolution** after Saad Zaghloul's deportation | India and Egypt |
| 13 April 1919 | **Amritsar (Jallianwala Bagh) massacre**: troops under General Dyer fire on an unarmed crowd | Punjab |
| May–August 1919 | **Third Anglo-Afghan War**; Afghanistan wins full control of its foreign policy | Afghanistan |
| June 1919 | Treaty of Versailles; dominions and India sign separately | Europe |
| 1919 | Seamen's riots against Black and Arab sailors in British ports | Britain |
| 1920 | **Iraqi Revolt**; San Remo conference confirms mandates; Gandhi launches Non-Cooperation; Government of Ireland Act partitions Ireland | Iraq, India, Ireland |
| 1920 | Somaliland Dervish state destroyed by RAF bombing | Somaliland |
| 1921 | **Malabar (Moplah) Rebellion**; Cairo Conference makes Faisal king of Iraq and Abdullah emir of Transjordan; **Anglo-Irish Treaty** (December) | India and Middle East |
| February 1922 | Chauri Chaura: protesters kill 22 police; Gandhi calls off Non-Cooperation | India |
| February 1922 | Britain unilaterally declares Egypt independent, with major reservations | Egypt |
| 1922 | Irish Free State created (December); Irish Civil War (1922–1923); Rand Revolt in South Africa; Harry Thuku protest shootings in Nairobi | Ireland, South Africa, Kenya |

| 1924 | British Empire Exhibition at Wembley | |

| 1930–1932 | Round Table Conferences in London | Gandhi attends the second (1931) |
| 1931 | **Statute of Westminster** | Legal independence of the dominions |
| 1932 | Ottawa Agreements set up imperial trade preferences; **Iraq independent** and joins the League of Nations | |
| 1934–1939 | **Labour rebellions across the British Caribbean**: Belize, St Kitts (1935), Barbados and Trinidad (1937), Jamaica (1938) | Lead to trade unions, the Moyne Commission and later the region's political parties |
| 1935 | Government of India Act | Provincial self-government; elections in 1937 |
| 1936 | Anglo-Egyptian Treaty; Edward VIII abdicates (December) | |
| 1936–1939 | **Arab Revolt in Palestine** | Several thousand Palestinians killed; harsh British counter-insurgency |
| 1936–1939 | Faqir of Ipi's campaign in Waziristan | Ties down tens of thousands of troops |
| 1937 | Peel Commission proposes partitioning Palestine; Burma separated from India | |
| 1938 | Munich Agreement | |

| 1915 | John Chilembwe | Nyasaland | Killed; now a national hero in Malawi |
| 1915 | Fifth Light Infantry | Singapore | 47 publicly executed |
| 1915 | Ghadar Party | Punjab | Plot betrayed; dozens hanged |
| 1916 | Irish Volunteers and Citizen Army | Dublin | 16 leaders executed, which turned opinion towards independence |
| 1919 | Egyptian Revolution | Egypt | Led to nominal independence in 1922 |
| 1919 | Rowlatt protests | Punjab | Amritsar massacre; martial law |

| 1920 | Iraqi Revolt | Iraq | Crushed with heavy use of air power; thousands of Iraqis killed |
| 1920–1922 | Non-Cooperation Movement | India | Called off after Chauri Chaura |

## Things that happened at the same time

- **Spring 1919.** In a few weeks: the Egyptian Revolution (March), the March First Movement in Korea against Japan (March), Amritsar (April), the May Fourth Movement in China (May), the Third Afghan War (May) and the start of the Irish War of Independence (January). Historians call it the "Wilsonian moment".
- **April 1916.** The Easter Rising and the surrender at Kut happened within days of each other. Britain's two worst setbacks of the spring were in Dublin and Mesopotamia.
- **1915–1917.** Britain promised Arab independence (Hussein–McMahon), agreed to divide the region with France (Sykes–Picot), and supported a Jewish national home (Balfour), all within two years.
- **1930.** The Salt March, the Chittagong raid, the Peshawar massacre and the Saya San rebellion all began within about eight months, while the Great Depression was crushing colonial commodity prices.
- **1935–1938.** Italy's invasion of Ethiopia, the Arab Revolt in Palestine and the Caribbean labour revolts overlapped. Protesters in Trinidad and Jamaica cited Ethiopia, linking anti-colonial causes across the world.

## Sources and flags

- Kim A. Wagner, *Amritsar 1919: An Empire of Fear and the Making of a Massacre* (2019).
- Erez Manela, *The Wilsonian Moment* (2007).
- Charles Townshend, *Easter 1916* (2005) and *The Republic: The Fight for Irish Independence* (2013).
- Santanu Das, *India, Empire, and First World War Culture* (2018).
- Commonwealth War Graves Commission: https://www.cwgc.org
- Rashid Khalidi, *The Hundred Years' War on Palestine* (2020).
- Richard Hart, *Rise and Organise* (1989), on the Caribbean labour revolts.
- **Flag:** Amritsar death tolls vary: the official Hunter Committee figure was 379 dead; the Indian National Congress inquiry estimated about 1,000. The influenza death toll in India is highly uncertain (12 to 20 million is the usual range). Empire-wide troop totals (about 8.7 million) are commonly cited approximations. The "largest extent" of the empire is usually given as about a quarter of the world's land and population around 1920–1922; exact figures depend on how mandates and protectorates are counted.
